```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE,
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110,
                      fig.align = "center")
library(staysvic)
library(ggplot2)

ink <- "#1B2A3A"; ocean <- "#1F6F8B"; coral <- "#D9644A"; muted <- "#6B7785"
theme_post <- theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title.position = "plot", legend.position = "top",
        legend.title = element_blank())

# Helpers that keep every sentence true whatever the data says
num <- function(x, d = 0) if (length(x) == 0 || is.na(x)) "not available" else format(round(x, d), nsmall = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x) if (length(x) == 0 || is.na(x)) "not available" else scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)
dol <- function(x) if (length(x) == 0 || is.na(x)) "not available" else scales::dollar(x, accuracy = 1)
compare <- function(a, b) {
  if (is.na(a) || is.na(b)) return("hard to compare with")
  r <- a / b
  if (r > 1.5) "much bigger than" else if (r > 1.1) "bigger than" else
    if (r >= 0.9) "about the same as" else if (r >= 0.67) "smaller than" else "much smaller than"
}

# The story follows one coastal town. Lorne if the data has it, otherwise
# the biggest Great Ocean Road town.
gor <- vic_listings[vic_listings$active & vic_listings$zone == "Great Ocean Road" &
                      !grepl("^Rest of", vic_listings$place), ]
town <- if ("Lorne" %in% gor$place) "Lorne" else names(sort(table(gor$place), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
compare_towns <- intersect(c(town, "Sorrento", "Torquay", "Apollo Bay"), unique(vic_listings$place))[1:3]
compare_towns <- compare_towns[!is.na(compare_towns)]

season <- seasonal_demand(compare_towns)
swing <- function(p) { s <- season[season$place == p, ]; if (nrow(s) == 0 || min(s$index) == 0) NA else max(s$index) / min(s$index) }
peak <- function(p) { s <- season[season$place == p, ]; if (nrow(s) == 0) NA else month.name[s$month[which.max(s$index)]] }
quiet <- function(p) { s <- season[season$place == p, ]; if (nrow(s) == 0) NA else month.name[s$month[which.min(s$index)]] }

hosts <- host_mix(town)
single <- function(p) hosts$share[hosts$place == p & hosts$host_tier == "Single listing"]
big <- function(p) hosts$share[hosts$place == p & hosts$host_tier == "10 or more listings"]
hotel <- function(p) hosts$hotel_share[hosts$place == p][1]

be_town <- breakeven_nights(town, bedrooms = 3)
be_cbd <- breakeven_nights("Melbourne CBD", bedrooms = 1)

snapshot <- format(max(vic_listings$snapshot), "%d %B %Y")
n_active <- sum(vic_listings$active)

# One-line verdicts chosen by the data, not written in advance
ratio <- swing(town) / swing("Melbourne CBD")
verdict_short <- if (is.na(ratio)) {
  "There is not enough data to say which market is steadier."
} else if (ratio > 1.1) {
  paste0("The CBD is the steadier market, while ", town, " depends much more on its busy season.")
} else if (ratio >= 0.9) {
  paste0("Surprisingly, ", town, " is about as steady through the year as the CBD.")
} else {
  paste0("Surprisingly, ", town, " is steadier through the year than the CBD.")
}
verdict_end <- if (is.na(ratio)) {
  "The data is too thin to say whether the coast is more seasonal than the city."
} else if (ratio > 1.1) {
  "The data backs up the hunch that the coast is more seasonal than the city."
} else {
  "The data does not back up the hunch that the coast is more seasonal than the city."
}
```

## The problem

Picture a three-bedroom house a short walk from the beach in `r town`. On a
Saturday in January it is booked months in advance, and the owner could
probably charge twice the usual rate and still fill it. Now picture the same
house on a wet Tuesday in July. The road is quiet, half the cafes have
shortened their hours, and the calendar is empty.

Now picture a one-bedroom unit on Collins Street. It never has a January like
that, but it also never has a July like that. Business travellers, concert
crowds and people in town for the footy keep it ticking over most of the year.

If you are thinking about buying a place to run as an Airbnb, or switching a
property you already own from a normal lease to short stays, those two
pictures are the whole decision. A coastal house can earn a lot in a few
months. A city unit earns less per night but more steadily. And in both
places you are competing with someone, sometimes a family renting out their
holiday home and sometimes a company running dozens of listings.

This post walks through the **staysvic** package and its app, which were
built to help with that decision. Along the way it answers three questions:

1. When is each place busy, and how does that compare with the CBD?
2. Who runs the short stays there?
3. How many booked nights would a short stay need to earn more than a normal lease?

<div style="border-left: 4px solid #1F6F8B; background: #EEF5F7; padding: 0.8rem 1rem; border-radius: 4px; margin: 1.5rem 0;">
**The short version.**
In `r town`, the busiest month for whole-home short stays is
`r peak(town)` and the quietest is `r quiet(town)`. The busiest month is
about `r num(swing(town), 1)` times as busy as the quietest. In the
Melbourne CBD that gap is `r num(swing("Melbourne CBD"), 1)` times.
A typical three-bedroom whole home in `r town` would need about
`r num(be_town$nights_needed)` booked nights a month to beat the median rent,
and the estimate for a typical listing there is about
`r num(be_town$est_nights_avg)` nights. `r verdict_short`
</div>

## Where the evidence comes from

The package uses two public datasets, both released under the Creative
Commons Attribution 4.0 licence.

**Inside Airbnb** ([insideairbnb.com](https://insideairbnb.com/get-the-data/))
collects every public Airbnb listing in a region every few months. This
package uses the snapshot from `r snapshot` for three Victorian regions:
Melbourne, the Mornington Peninsula, and Barwon South West, which is the one
that covers Geelong, the Bellarine and the Great Ocean Road. After cleaning,
there are `r num(n_active)` active listings, meaning listings that had at
least one guest review in the past year.

**The Homes Victoria Rental Report**
([data.vic.gov.au](https://discover.data.vic.gov.au/dataset/rental-report-quarterly-moving-annual-rents-by-suburb))
gives the median weekly rent for new leases by council area and dwelling
type. This is the "normal lease" that a short stay is compared with.

Inside Airbnb only says which council area a listing is in. That is too
coarse for this question, because the Surf Coast council covers Torquay,
Anglesea and Lorne, which are very different markets. So each listing is also
matched to the nearest town centre if it sits within a few kilometres of one.
The towns are listed in `vic_places`.

```{r regions}
tab <- as.data.frame(table(vic_listings$zone[vic_listings$active]))
names(tab) <- c("Area", "Active listings")
tab <- tab[order(-tab$`Active listings`), ]
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Table 1: Active listings in each area of the package.")
```

## Installing the package and opening the app

The package lives on GitHub. Install it once, then load it and launch the app.

```{r install, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("etc5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-devaansh-ops")

library(staysvic)
run_app()
```

The app opens in your browser with four tabs. **Start here** explains who the
app is for and defines the terms. The other three tabs each answer one of the
questions above. The CBD is always on the charts as a baseline, so every town
is judged against a market most people already know.

```{r screenshot-start, out.width = "100%"}
if (file.exists("figures/app-start.png")) knitr::include_graphics("figures/app-start.png")
```

## A few words first

You don't need any background for these. Table 2 explains the terms the app
uses, and the rest of the post sticks to them.

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| Short stay | A listing that accepts stays shorter than 28 nights. Victoria's short stay levy uses the same line. |
| Mid stay | A listing with a minimum stay of 28 nights or more. These hosts use Airbnb more like a rental site. |
| Entire home | The guest gets the whole house or unit. |
| Active listing | A listing with at least one guest review in the last 12 months. |
| Demand | Counted with guest reviews, because Airbnb does not publish bookings. |
| Place | A town, or a council area for listings that are not near any listed town. |

Table: Table 2: Terms used in the app and in this post.

Demand needs a little more explanation, because it is the number the rest of
the app leans on. Guests can only review a place after they have stayed
there, so a month with lots of reviews is a month with lots of stays. Not
every guest writes one, so the count is always lower than the real number of
stays. That is fine for spotting *when* a place is busy, which is what the
first tab is about.

## Question 1: when is it busy?

The **When is it busy?** tab has three controls. Pick up to four towns to
compare with the CBD. Choose short stays, mid stays or both. Choose entire
homes, private rooms or anything.

The chart shows each month compared with that place's own average month. A
value of 2 means twice as busy as usual and 0.5 means half as busy. This puts
a small town and the whole CBD on the same scale, so you can compare their
*shape* rather than their size. Figure 1 is the same chart, drawn for
`r paste(compare_towns, collapse = ", ")`.

```{r fig-season, fig.cap = "Figure 1: Demand through the year for whole-home short stays, compared with each place's average month. The dashed grey line is the Melbourne CBD."}
towns_df <- season[season$place != "Melbourne CBD", ]
cbd_df <- season[season$place == "Melbourne CBD", ]
ggplot(towns_df, aes(month_label, index, colour = place, group = place)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "#C9BFAF") +
  geom_line(data = cbd_df, linetype = "dashed", colour = muted, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(ocean, coral, "#E0A526")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "x")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Compared with an average month") +
  theme_post
```

In `r town`, demand peaks in `r peak(town)` and bottoms out in
`r quiet(town)`. The busiest month is about `r num(swing(town), 1)` times as
busy as the quietest. The CBD's swing is `r num(swing("Melbourne CBD"), 1)`
times, so the seasonal gap in `r town` is
`r compare(swing(town), swing("Melbourne CBD"))` the CBD's.

This is where the app earns its place over a static chart. Every town has its
own rhythm, and the town a reader cares about is rarely the one a report
happens to print. Swapping towns in and out, or switching from entire homes
to private rooms, shows straight away whether a pattern holds.

The table under the chart sums each place up in one row: busiest month,
quietest month and the swing between them.

## Question 2: who runs it?

The **Who runs it?** tab takes one place and compares who operates its active
listings with who operates them in the CBD. Hosts are sorted by how many
listings they run across the three regions:

- **Single listing.** Usually an owner renting out their own home or holiday house.
- **2 to 9 listings.** Small investors or friends-and-family managers.
- **10 or more listings.** Almost always a management company.

```{r fig-hosts, fig.height = 2.6, fig.cap = "Figure 2: Share of active listings by how many listings the host runs."}
h <- hosts
h$place <- factor(h$place, levels = rev(unique(h$place)))
ggplot(h, aes(share, place, fill = host_tier)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#9CC5D1", ocean, ink)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.04))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_post + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

In `r town`, `r pct(single(town))` of active listings are run by a host with
just one listing, and `r pct(big(town))` by hosts running ten or more. In the
CBD those shares are `r pct(single("Melbourne CBD"))` and
`r pct(big("Melbourne CBD"))`. Hotel rooms and serviced apartments make up
`r pct(hotel(town))` of `r town`'s Airbnb listings and
`r pct(hotel("Melbourne CBD"))` of the CBD's.

Why does this matter to someone starting out? A market full of single
hosts is one where a newcomer competes with people like themselves. A market
dominated by companies means competing with professional photos, dynamic
pricing and hundreds of reviews. The app also lists the biggest operators in
each place by name. Only hosts with ten or more listings are named, because
those are businesses. Smaller hosts are private people and stay anonymous.

One thing this tab cannot do is compare Airbnb with hotels. There is no
open, current dataset of hotel bookings for Victorian towns, so the most the
app can say is how much of Airbnb itself is made up of hotel rooms.

## Question 3: does it pay?

The **Does it pay?** tab brings it together. Pick a place and a number of
bedrooms. The app fills in the Homes Victoria median weekly rent for that
council area, which you can type over with your own figure. A slider sets the
share of each night's price you would lose to platform fees, cleaning and
management. It starts at 20 per cent.

The app then works out how many booked nights a month you would need to earn
the same as a normal lease:

$$\text{nights needed} = \frac{\text{weekly rent} \times 52 / 12}{\text{nightly price} \times (1 - \text{costs})}$$

The bars in Figure 3 estimate how many nights a typical listing in that place
was actually booked each month last year. To get from reviews to nights, the
app uses the same rough rule Inside Airbnb uses: about half of guests leave a
review, and a typical stay is about three nights.

```{r fig-breakeven, fig.cap = paste0("Figure 3: Estimated booked nights a month for a typical whole-home listing in ", town, ", against the nights a three-bedroom home would need to match the median rent (red line).")}
m <- be_town$monthly[[1]]
if (nrow(m) > 0) {
  p <- ggplot(m, aes(month_label, est_nights)) +
    geom_col(fill = ocean, width = 0.7) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimated nights booked") + theme_post
  if (!is.na(be_town$nights_needed)) p <- p +
    geom_hline(yintercept = be_town$nights_needed, colour = coral, linewidth = 1.1)
  p
}
```

For a three-bedroom whole home in `r town`, the median nightly price is
`r dol(be_town$median_price)`, based on `r be_town$n_listings` active
listings. Against a weekly rent of `r dol(be_town$weekly_rent)`
(`r be_town$rent_source`), it would need about
`r num(be_town$nights_needed)` booked nights a month to break even. A typical
listing there gets an estimated `r num(be_town$est_nights_avg)` nights, rising
to `r num(be_town$est_nights_peak)` in `r be_town$peak_month` and falling to
`r num(be_town$est_nights_low)` in `r be_town$low_month`.

For a one-bedroom unit in the CBD, the break-even point is about
`r num(be_cbd$nights_needed)` nights against an estimated
`r num(be_cbd$est_nights_avg)` nights for a typical listing.

The useful part is moving the sliders. Push costs from 20 to 30 per cent, or
type in a rent you think is realistic, and watch the red line move. If the
answer flips with a small change, the decision is closer than any single
number makes it look.

## When the data is thin

Some combinations simply do not have enough listings to say anything
reliable. A four-bedroom home in a small town might have two listings, and a
median of two prices is not much of a median. Rather than show a confident
number, the app says so. Here is the note it gives for a case like that:

```{r weak, echo = TRUE}
small <- names(sort(table(vic_listings$place[vic_listings$active])))[1]
breakeven_nights(small, bedrooms = 4)$note
```

The first tab does the same for places with fewer than 100 reviews, and the
second warns when a place has fewer than 30 active listings.

## What a would-be host should do next

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Compare shapes | In *When is it busy?*, put your town next to the CBD. | A big swing means most of the year's money comes in a few weeks. |
| 2. Check the competition | In *Who runs it?*, look at the share of big operators. | Competing with companies is harder on price and reviews. |
| 3. Test the break-even | In *Does it pay?*, enter a rent you could really get. | The median rent is a starting point, not your property. |
| 4. Stress the costs | Move the cost slider up to 30 per cent. | Cleaning and management often cost more than people expect. |
| 5. Look at the quiet months | Compare the low bars with the red line. | Those are the months you need savings for. |

Table: Table 3: A five-step way to use the app before making a decision.

A few things the app does not support. It does not predict future bookings.
It does not account for mortgage costs, council rates, insurance or the
7.5 per cent short stay levy that is added to each booking. And it does not know
anything about your particular property, which might be much better or worse
than the median.

## Limits

Two limits matter most. First, reviews are a stand-in for bookings. The
"half of guests review" rule is a rough average, and the real share could
be higher in some towns and lower in others. That changes the size of the
booked-nights estimate, though not the shape of the seasonal pattern.
Second, Inside Airbnb publishes one year of free snapshots, and each listing's
settings are taken from the newest one. A host who changed their minimum stay
during the year is counted under their current setting for every month.

## Conclusion

Back to the beach house in `r town` and the unit on Collins Street.
`r verdict_end` Demand in `r town` swings by
about `r num(swing(town), 1)` times between its best and worst months, which
is `r compare(swing(town), swing("Melbourne CBD"))` the CBD's
`r num(swing("Melbourne CBD"), 1)` times. Whether a short stay beats a normal
lease comes down to whether the busy months earn enough to carry the quiet
ones, and the app lets you test that for your own town, size and costs. Used
that way, it will not make the decision for you, but it will show you where
the decision is close.

<details>
<summary><strong>Behind the post: how this differs from the app</strong></summary>

This post and the app use the same functions and the same data, but they do
different jobs. The post tells one story about one town. The app lets a
reader tell their own.

|  | This post | The app |
|---|---|---|
| Who it is for | Someone deciding whether the app is worth opening | Someone working through their own decision |
| Places | One coastal town and the CBD | Any town, up to four at once |
| Numbers | Fixed at the default settings | Change with rent, costs and bedrooms |
| Charts | Three, each answering one question | The same three, redrawn on every change |

Three choices shape the writing. A story
opening makes a dry money question easier to care about. Background comes
before numbers, so readers can judge them. And in a data story the headline
result goes early, so people keep reading.

On the charts, each one carries a single message. Soft colours keep the page
calm, and the CBD always appears as the same dashed grey line so the eye
learns to read it as the baseline.

</details>
